FAST

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nine measles-related deaths in the United States this year, as the country battles its worst outbreak of the highly contagious viral infection in decades. The US had recorded 6,039 confirmed measles cases as of Nov 24, across 47 jurisdictions, according to the agency's website on Wednesday. That includes 18 cases among international visitors. The CDC updated its tally after the National Center for Health Statistics received additional reports from states and verified that the deaths had occurred and that measles was the underlying cause, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said. Based on publicly reported state figures, however, the US has recorded at least 14 measles-associated deaths this year, including nine fatalities in Pennsylvania, three in Wisconsin and one each in Virginia and New York state.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose earlier this year after CDC, under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures. "The discrepancy between state and federal measles-related death figures is concerning and risks confusing the public about the true toll of this outbreak," said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and CEO of the Center of Science and Industry. "Regardless of the precise number, these deaths are alarming and reflect the consequences of declining vaccination coverage," Bertley said. Cases in the US have reached a 35-year high, a resurgence driven largely by unvaccinated people that this month stripped the country of its hard-fought measles elimination status . CDC data showed that 671 patients, or 11 per cent of confirmed cases, were hospitalised, with children aged under 5 years recording the highest hospitalisation rate at 17 per cent. The agency also said the death count could change as it reviews additional information. On Wednesday, Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported 1,679 measles cases so far this year, including 87 new cases over the past seven days and 340 hospitalisations.

Israeli judges have recommended dropping one of three corruption cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsidering another, in a trial that began in 2020.

JERUSALEM: Israeli judges on Wednesday (Nov 25) recommended that prosecutors drop one of three long-running cases against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and reconsider another alleging he granted favours in exchange for positive media coverage. Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust. He denies the charges and has pleaded not guilty. His trial began in 2020 and involves three criminal cases. In the case referred to as Case 4000, prosecutors allege that Netanyahu granted regulatory favours worth around 1.8 billion shekels (about US$500 million) to Bezeq Telecom Israel. In return, prosecutors say, he sought positive coverage for himself and his wife, Sara, on a news website controlled by former Bezeq Chairman Shaul Elovitch. Elovitch has denied wrongdoing. In a blow to prosecutors, Judge Rivka Friedman-Feldman of Jerusalem District Court , who presides over Case 4000, told Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara at a hearing on Wednesday that a conviction was unlikely and the case should be dropped.

The recommendation was not a ruling on the case, the court clarified, and Baharav-Miara said she would review the court's statements with the prosecution. The judges also recommended prosecutors reconsider so-called Case 2000 because of doubts that Netanyahu's actions constituted a criminal offence. In that case, prosecutors allege Netanyahu negotiated a deal with Arnon Mozes, owner of Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper, for better coverage in return for legislation to slow the growth of a rival newspaper. Netanyahu on Wednesday called the court's recommendation a "ray of light for truth and justice." "Ten years of suffering for dozens of my close ones who were dragged into interrogation rooms," Netanyahu said in a televised address. "Where they were blackmailed with criminal acts, humiliated, and the lives of many of them were ruined, just so they would give false testimony against me."

BERLIN: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz accused Russia on Wednesday (Nov 25) of "escalating" threats to European security as he defended his government's plans to bolster defence spending and maintain financial aid to Ukraine. Opposition parties, including t he far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which tops national opinion polls, and t he hard-left Die Linke, have called for an end to military aid to Kyiv . "It cannot be s aid often enough, against t he far right as much as t he far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants . And Russia wants more than Ukraine," Merz told t he Bundestag lower house of parliament during a debate on t he 2027 draft budget. "Russia is escalating in t he Baltic region, in Poland, on t he Black Sea; Russia is escalating in space, and Russia is by now also escalating massively he re in our own country," he s aid .

Russia did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on Merz 's accusations. It has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries and says its actions in Ukraine are aimed at protecting its own national security. Merz 's government blamed Russia in September for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport , an accusation t he Russian Embassy in Berlin dismissed as part of a "new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany". Germany and ot he r European countries have also been hit by a wave of cyberattacks and sabotage incidents targeting critical infrastructure that t he y have often blamed on Russia. Moscow has denied all t he allegations.

"LEARNING FROM UKRAINE" Merz s aid on Wednesday that by supporting Ukraine, Germany was also protecting itself. "We are learning from Ukraine - technologically for civilian use but of course also in defence technology," he s aid . Germany has been Ukraine's biggest military backer in Europe since Russia's full-blown invasion on Feb 24, 2022, but public support for this policy has decreased amid cost-of-living pressures. A poll publis he d on Tuesday showed a narrow majority of Germans now oppose giving military aid to Kyiv . "Whose chancellor are you, actually?" AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla asked Merz during Wednesday's debate, accusing the government of supporting Ukraine while failing to provide sufficient relief to German citizens. "What a mockery!" Germany aims to double defence spending to over €200 billion (US$228 billion) between now and 2030, according to t he 2027 draft budget, hitting 3.7 per cent of national output by 2030, in line with commitments to NATO.

EU SHOULD FOCUS ON SECURITY AND COMPETITIVENESS, MERZ SAYS Merz also addressed on Wednesday t he latest proposal for t he European Union budget for 2028-2034 presented by European Council chief Antonio Costa. Costa proposed cuts that would reduce t he overall seven-year budget to €1.582 trillion, some €40 billion less than a proposal presented by t he Irish EU presidency in October. EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposals at a special summit on Thursday and Friday. "In t he se negotiations I am pushing for spending to be limited and focused on what really makes Europe stronger: security and competitiveness," Merz s aid . "If spending is focused, it is t he best additional insurance for our country."

NEW YORK: The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Wednesday (Nov 25) amid a tech selloff, but finished well off the day's lows as bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday. The Dow finished higher. The Nasdaq fell more than 4 per cent early in the session as the selloff in AI-related stocks and new US tariff proposals hit sentiment. "There are all these potential headwinds, but then there's also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that's part of what we're seeing," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut.

"The broad selloffs tend to kind of throw the baby out with the bathwater. Investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies," he said. Technology and consumer discretionary fell 1 per cent each and led declines among S&P 500 sectors, while materials and real estate led gainers . Value stocks outperformed growth, with the Russell 1000 value index up 0.4 per cent and the Russell 1000 growth index down 0.8 per cent. Wall Street has been roiled this month, partly because of worries about AI leader Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO earlier this month, but the company's board reinstated him on Monday. The Nasdaq Composite is down 7.3 per cent for the month. "This has broadly been a more sentiment-driven type of selloff," said Charlie Ripley, senior investment strategist at Allianz Investment Management. At the same time, for some companies from a price-to-earnings perspective, "things are starting to look more attractive", he said. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 164.25 points, or 0.33 per cent, to 50,182.95, the S&P 500 lost 18.31 points, or 0.25 per cent, to 7,182.78 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 147.73 points, or 0.62 per cent, to 23,585.80. The market will be closed on Thursday and will close early on Friday.

AI WORRIES LINGER Nvidia shares fell 3.9 per cent and an index of semiconductors was off 0.7 per cent, while shares of Amazon fell 3.1 per cent. On the plus side, PC maker HP gained 11.5 per cent after it reported fourth-quarter revenue and profit above analysts' estimates. Fears of increased regulatory scrutiny of the AI sector following the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections have added to worries about AI stocks . Early in the day, the Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 per cent from its record closing high, flirting with bear-market territory. New tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have risen steadily due to the Iran war. The US proposed tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions In addition, investors digested data showing the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month and again in early 2027. "Tariffs are somewhat responsible for inflation ... so that's actually being counterproductive to what the Fed is trying to do," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York. Volume was lower than average for part of the session. Trading on US exchanges ended at about 22 billion shares.

CAIRO: Israel's military killed a senior Hamas security official as well as his wife and two children with an airstrike on their Gaza Strip apartment early on Wednesday (Nov 25), Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry and medics said. The airstrike that killed Mohammad Abuelouf, a Hamas colonel who heads the militants' interior security service, and his family was the second Israeli attack to kill a senior Hamas security official in the past 24 hours. Despite a year-old ceasefire, Israel has continued to carry out attacks that it says target Hamas but have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by United States President Donald Trump, has failed to halt the violence or secure Hamas' disarmament. Medics said the airstrike ripped through Abuelouf's apartment early on Wednesday in the Beach refugee camp in western Gaza City, near the coast. Later in the morning, another Israeli airstrike hit Gaza City's northern Karama neighbourhood, killing one person, medics said.

On Tuesday, after the military killed Naeem Abu Nahel, Hamas' head of internal security, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there was no escape for Hamas from his country's "long reach". Hamas' internal security service, which Abu Nahel ran and in which Abuelouf was a senior official, counters Palestinians suspected of collaboration with Israel's secret service and gathers information about its plans. At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was struck in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies. Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of Gaza, up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza's coast. Israel's assault on Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians since 2023, caused a hunger crisis, internally displaced Gaza's entire population and led to assessments of genocide from scholars and United Nations inquiries. Israel has said its actions were in self-defence after Hamas-led militants killed 1,200 people and took more than 250 hostages in an attack on Israel in October 2023.

WASHINGTON: United States President Donald Trump on Wednesday (Nov 25) fired a new tariff salvo on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, the European Union and Singapore, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses his Republican Party suffered in US midterm elections . His administration proposed new headline tariff rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent, but said duties would be capped at lower levels agreed under trade deals that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation. Under the main "Section 301" probe into excess industrial capacity, China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term. That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on January 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent, the United States Trade Representative (USTR) said.

Vietnam would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with Washington, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs, which would not take effect until after a Jan 25 public hearing, were intended to counteract "industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labour suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices" that undermine the US manufacturing base. Washington has long accused China of subsidising industry and flooding global markets with low-cost exports ranging from steel to electric vehicles and solar products. Beijing earlier reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and rejected allegations of overcapacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation. "FALSE ISSUE", CHINA SAYS "The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's top two economies to maintain stable relations. The USTR also proposed capped tariff rates of 18 per cent for imported goods from Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh, and 15 per cent, including existing "Most Favored Nation" duties, for Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, the EU and Switzerland. India, which has yet to reach a trade deal with the Trump administration, would face a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail, the USTR said.  The USTR proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent, taking into account existing Section 301 tariffs, on Singapore goods, with exemptions for certain goods, it said in a press release. It further proposed an adjusted tariff rate of 10 per cent to account for the event that Singapore were to reach an agreement on reciprocal trade with the US, or conclude other negotiated agreements that address the concerns raised by the US investigation into Singapore’s policies and practices. Greer told CNBC the proposed caps were consistent with trade agreements reached over the past year that also lowered barriers to US exports. "We're sticking to that in terms of our proposals because we think a lot of these deals we made actually solve a lot of the problems we see in excess capacity or can go toward it," Greer said. "So you know we've talked to our trading partners about this. They know what we're proposing. I think a lot of this is baked in." Mexico and Norway were excluded from the proposals because investigations into their trade practices remain under way, Greer said. Even so, the prospect of new trade barriers weighed on stock markets on Wednesday amid a renewed sell-off in tech stocks. Major US indexes opened down more than 1 per cent, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq composite down more than 3 per cent. "It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind," ING analysts wrote. Separately, the USTR proposed a new 10 per cent tariff on imports of Brazil's finished Embraer commercial aircraft, and to raise duties on imports of Brazilian sugar that exceed quotas as part of an effort to push Brasilia to rectify alleged unfair trade practices. The products were previously exempted from Trump's 25 per cent tariffs on Brazilian goods that were imposed in July. A US official said that despite negotiations, there were "substantial differences" over the allegations.

Related:

China warns US against imposing new tariffs

Courtesy for courtesy, curbs for curbs? The two sides of Trump-Xi reciprocity

NEW DUTIES WON'T EXCEED NEGOTIATED LIMITS Trump's tariffs have contributed to higher prices for US consumers, and a Reuters-Ipsos opinion poll conducted after Republicans' midterm losses found 62 per cent of respondents supported efforts to repeal them. But Trump has long vowed to restore duties struck down by the US Supreme Court in February. The latest measures follow an eight-month investigation into unfair trade practices under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Greer said the proposed tariffs would not apply to about US$30 billion of Chinese imports under consideration for tariff reductions through a bilateral mechanism known as the Board of Trade. However, the new duties would be added to tariffs imposed on Chinese goods during Trump's first term, which total roughly 25 per cent. They would not be imposed on top of the 10 per cent and 12.5 per cent tariffs introduced in July on a broader group of 60 trading partners over allegations of lax enforcement of anti-forced-labour laws. Analysts said higher US trade barriers against China and other economies are the direction of travel, even if the Democratic Party - which won majorities in both houses of Congress earlier this month - tried to curb Trump's tariff impulses. "Without the two-thirds majority needed to override a presidential veto, Democrats' ability to dismantle the tariff wall will remain limited," ING analysts said in a note. "Either way, we don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps." The US-China truce runs until Jan 10, but many expect it to be extended - potentially as early as next month when Trump and Xi are set to meet again at a Group of Twenty gathering in Miami - given the major impact a re-escalation of tit-for-tat hikes similar to those seen in 2025 would have on both economies. The USTR's investigation is also partly directed at Chinese investment in Southeast Asian countries, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Cambodia, to manufacture goods for the US market and avoid prior US tariffs.

JAKARTA: Three people have died while search and rescue operations are currently underway for an "estimated" 23 more workers trapped in a mine in West Java province on Wednesday (Nov 25), authorities said.  The miners have been stuck in a mine 100m deep since Monday as heavy rains inundated access, the search and rescue agency said, adding access was narrow and the terrain was slippery and dark.  "The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement. The agency said the first body was recovered at 12.20pm (local time), followed by the second at 12.35pm and the third at 1.48pm.

"All three were recovered from Shaft A at a depth of around 30m to 40m and were confirmed dead. Their identities have yet to be established," said Desiana.

The Jakarta SAR Office is coordinating with joint rescue teams to monitor flooding and assess access to the mine shaft in Kampung Ciguha, Nanggung, Bogor Regency. (Photo: Basarnas)

The agency said it was pumping water out of the mine shaft to support search and evacuation efforts. The mine is located in the Pongkor area of Bogor, a mountainous area 60km south of the capital Jakarta.

Rescue teams work at the site of a mine where workers were trapped after heavy rains inundated access. (Photo: Basarnas)

State miner Antam, which operates gold mining operations in Pongkor, said the incident occurred at an unauthorised gold mine and was not a part of its operations.  Small-scale and illegal mining has often caused accidents in resource-rich Indonesia, where mineral resources are located in remote areas in conditions difficult for authorities to regulate. Authorities closed around 30 gold mine pits last week in a separate area in Bogor, news website Detik reported.
